prompt: A server receives a request for /order?id=4471&user_id=102 and returns that order's data without checking whether the currently logged-in session actually belongs to user 102. What security concept does this illustrate?
choices: The server is trusting client-supplied input without verifying it
TLS has failed to encrypt the request
The DNS resolver has been poisoned
The session cookie is missing the Secure flag

prompt: You visit https://paypa1-secure-login.com and your browser shows a valid padlock with no warnings. What does that padlock actually guarantee?
choices: The site is operated by PayPal
The site's content is safe and free of malware
You have an encrypted, tamper-evident connection to whoever holds the private key for that exact domain
The site has been verified as legitimate by your browser vendor

prompt: Which of the following is TLS/HTTPS explicitly NOT designed to protect against?
choices: An attacker on the same coffee-shop Wi-Fi reading your traffic in plaintext
A man-in-the-middle silently modifying your HTTP response in transit
A SQL injection vulnerability in the legitimate server's own application code
Someone spoofing the identity of the certificate's claimed domain without the matching private key

prompt: After you log in, your browser sends a session cookie on every subsequent request. What is the server actually relying on to treat you as 'logged in'?
choices: Your password being resubmitted and rechecked on every request
Your IP address matching the one used at login
Possession of the exact session identifier string, checked against its session store
The TLS certificate presented by your browser

prompt: An attacker successfully reads a logged-in user's session cookie value through an XSS flaw and sends it in their own request to the server. What is the most accurate description of the result?
choices: Nothing happens, because the server also checks the original password
The server treats the attacker's request as authenticated, equivalent to stealing that user's login
The request is rejected because the cookie's HttpOnly flag blocks reuse
The server detects the new IP address and forces a fresh login automatically

prompt: Which cookie attribute specifically prevents JavaScript (document.cookie) from reading a session cookie's value, blunting basic XSS-based theft?
choices: Secure
SameSite
HttpOnly
Max-Age

prompt: Running `dig +trace example.com` shows your query walking through root servers, the .com TLD servers, and example.com's authoritative nameserver. By default, what security property does this plain DNS lookup have?
choices: It is cryptographically signed and authenticated end-to-end by default
It travels encrypted over TLS by default
It is unauthenticated and spoofable unless DNSSEC or DNS-over-HTTPS is explicitly used
DNS answers cannot be forged because they always match the domain in the browser's address bar

prompt: An nmap scan of a lab VM shows ports 21 (FTP), 22 (SSH), 80 (HTTP), and 3306 (MySQL) all open. Why does this matter from a security standpoint, beyond just being a technical inventory?
choices: It means the VM has four separate running services, each a piece of code that can be sent attacker-controlled input
Open ports are purely informational and have no bearing on risk
Only port 3306 matters because databases are the only attackable service
It confirms the VM is already compromised
